title: Markets, Fairs, and the Trade That Sustained Skala
summary: Trade and commerce connected Skala to nearby villages and distant markets, revealing how the town made its living.
editorialContent:
![Skala-Podilska, the frontier town whose markets connected local producers and merchants](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/%D0%A1%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0-%D0%9F%D0%BE%D0%B4%D1%96%D0%BB%D1%8C%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%BB_%D0%92%D0%BE%D0%B7%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%96%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8F_%D0%94%D1%96%D0%B2%D0%B8_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%96%D1%97.jpg/1920px-%D0%A1%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0-%D0%9F%D0%BE%D0%B4%D1%96%D0%BB%D1%8C%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B0_%D0%9A%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B5%D0%BB_%D0%92%D0%BE%D0%B7%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%96%D0%BD%D0%BD%D1%8F_%D0%94%D1%96%D0%B2%D0%B8_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%80%D1%96%D1%97.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A town connected by trade

In the [Skala Jewish community](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40), trade was not one occupation among many. It linked the town’s Jewish shops and exporters to nearby villages, neighboring fairs, markets across the border, and customers as far away as western Europe and the Americas. The memorial book remembers a varied economy: peddlers and shopkeepers, grain buyers, carriers, clerks, exporters and artisans. It also makes clear that prosperity was uneven. Large businesses stood alongside people who depended on small sales and seasonal work.

Skala’s position on the Zbrucz River, on the former border between Austrian Galicia and the Russian Empire, helped shape this economy. The memorial book describes the town as a frontier place with a customs house, where lawful commerce and smuggling developed side by side. The [Yad Vashem place entry for Skala](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/places/5440531) independently records its changing political setting and its 1921 population: 1,555 Jews among 4,017 residents. The border, however, was not simply a line on a map. It offered commercial opportunities—and, as political control tightened, it could close them.

## Fair days and the weekly rhythm

The memorial book recalls a Wednesday weekly fair that drew thousands of peasants from surrounding villages. It does not identify the fair’s exact site, so its location remains uncertain. The fair brought rural buyers and sellers into town, giving local Jewish merchants access to agricultural produce while allowing them to sell goods to customers from outside Skala. The marketplace’s [weekly fair](/communities/skala/records/mention_0046764e01e30a5de8ec8a5e) was part of a regional routine, not an isolated event.

Skala’s traders also traveled out. The book says many merchants selling fabrics, clothing, leather goods, shoes and boots divided their week between their shops and fairs in neighboring towns. One important destination was [Olashkovtse, also called Lashkevitz](/communities/skala/records/mention_b2ce37def2c139cb780636f6), whose annual fair was widely advertised across eastern Galicia. Skala merchants held prominent places there. The book preserves a saying comparing great noise to “the Lashkewitz fair”—a small piece of local humor that hints at how large and familiar the gathering was.

Fairs supported more than the people standing behind stalls. Buyers needed carriers; goods needed carts and drivers; businesses relied on bookkeepers and clerks. Shopkeepers depended on the traffic, while artisans supplied the clothes, shoes, tools and household goods being sold. The book’s portrait of commerce is therefore also a portrait of work distributed across many households.

## From village produce to distant markets

Agricultural goods moved through Skala in large quantities. The memorial book describes Jewish merchants buying grain, beans, fodder and eggs from the surrounding countryside, then selling or exporting them. Wheat, rye, oats and barley supported a chain of buyers, carters, watchmen, porters and clerks. The book also says that Skala’s merchants exported legumes and flax to destinations including Germany, Switzerland, Italy, France, England and Spain, and farther overseas to the United States, Cuba and Puerto Rico. The records name the [United States](/communities/skala/records/mention_e31c2ea65c92a5295572174b), [Italy](/communities/skala/records/mention_6a46c1a6a19df9e2766ef555), [Cuba](/communities/skala/records/mention_a5441ea13973e95d30c68d40) and [Puerto Rico](/communities/skala/records/mention_462ffa89fe945511baf6299c) among the overseas connections.

The egg trade had its own local history. The book identifies [Kalman Bilgaray](/communities/skala/records/mention_d46c446a4eea73b9d3fad9d5) as Skala’s first egg exporter, and says [Berish Peper](/communities/skala/records/mention_765281b25c6cbd1faa98e8f6), who came from [Husiatin](/communities/skala/records/mention_df60b8804609c70b0046fbcf), later established an egg-export business. It also names [Israel Zeidman](/communities/skala/records/mention_c1fd0017212db460a3bbb5dd) as a principal exporter, associated with Yosef Weintraub, Eliezer Shenberg and Efraim Klinger. These records preserve a shift from an individual described as the first exporter to a trade involving multiple merchants and associates. They do not specify the precise dates, scale of each business, or whether the named exporters handled the same routes.

An independent personal account helps show how the trade worked at a local level. Menachem Bartel recalled that his father, Avraham Bretschneider, sold eggs for a company with an egg-collection center in Skala; the eggs went to Tarnopol or Lvov, and the company also exported. Bartel’s testimony adds a collection-and-distribution step not described in the book’s short notices about exporters. It does not establish a connection between Bretschneider and Bilgaray, Peper or Zeidman, so they should not be assumed to have belonged to the same firm. ([Bartel’s testimony](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/SkalaPodol/Bartel.html))

## A border economy—and its vulnerabilities

Before the First World War, trade across the Russian-Galician frontier involved both permitted goods and smuggling. The memorial book describes merchants, money-changers and moneylenders as part of the wider network around smugglers. It also recalls open crossings for duty-free products at the Zbrucz. The historical summary in *Pinkas Hakehillot Polin*, available through JewishGen, likewise describes Skala’s border trade and the importance of fairs and wholesale goods. Because that page is another memorial-community account rather than independent confirmation of the Skala book, it is useful for comparison, not as separate proof.

After the First World War, the border became increasingly restrictive. *Pinkas Hakehillot Polin* says that Polish and Soviet authorities limited cross-border movement and that the Soviet Union eventually closed the border. Wholesale egg, grain and legume businesses continued, but ordinary fair traders and shopkeepers faced heavy taxes and competition from Polish and Ukrainian cooperatives. This distinction matters: exporters with larger networks could continue operating, while small merchants whose livelihood depended on fairs were more exposed to changing rules and competition.

By the 1930s, the trade that had sustained Skala was under strain. The memorial book remembers a town in which rural exchange and overseas export existed side by side, but also one where a fair’s bustle could not guarantee a merchant’s security. In 1939 Soviet rule brought another rupture: Bartel recalled that private trade was prohibited and goods were confiscated. The old marketplace economy was not merely disrupted; its underlying conditions were overturned.

## The people behind the network

Skala’s commerce connected Jewish merchants to a predominantly rural region and to markets far beyond it. The names preserved in the memorial book—Bilgaray, Peper, Zeidman and his associates—give that network human scale, while the record of fairs, carriers and clerks shows how many more people depended on it. The trade was never simply “exports”: it began with produce from nearby farms, passed through local collection and transport, and relied on customers and intermediaries across shifting borders.

Important questions remain open. The memorial book does not give the first exporter’s business dates or explain how the egg firms were organized. Nor does the Wednesday-fair reference identify its precise location. Those gaps are not reasons to fill in a tidy story; they are invitations to pursue the [egg exporters’ business records](research:Kalman Bilgaray and Berish Peper egg-export businesses), the [Wednesday fair’s location](research:Location of Skala’s Wednesday weekly fair), and the firm remembered by [Avraham Bretschneider](research:Egg-collection company employing Avraham Bretschneider in Skala).
